summary.text: The second assertion fails at \(n=1408\): an exhaustive check of \(1\le k<1408\) computes \(\phi(1408-k)/2\) and uses modular exponentiation to exhibit a proper divisor of each resulting value, except for the few values that are directly \(<2\). Thus none of the 1407 admissible choices of \(k\) yields a prime.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the second assertion of the conjunction.  The counterexample is
\[
        n=1408.
\]
For this value of \(n\), no integer \(k\) with \(0<k<1408\) makes
\[
        (k+1)^{\phi(1408-k)/2}-k
\]
prime.  Since \(1408>5\), this is enough to disprove the stated conjunction, regardless of whether its first assertion about \(a(n)\) is true.

Here is the complete finite argument.  For \(1\leq k\leq 1407\), put
\[
 q_k=1408-k,\qquad e_k=\left\lfloor\frac{\phi(q_k)}2\right\rfloor,
 \qquad N_k=(k+1)^{e_k}-k.
\]
(The floor is relevant only when \(q_k=1\) or \(2\); for every \(q_k>2\), \(\phi(q_k)\) is even.)  We shall show that every \(N_k\) is nonprime.

We first describe the finite arithmetic calculation used below, including how each of its entries can be reproduced without constructing the enormous powers themselves.

For a positive integer \(q\), its totient was calculated from its prime factorization by
\[
  q=\prod p_i^{a_i}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \phi(q)=\prod p_i^{a_i-1}(p_i-1)
          =q\prod_{p_i\mid q}\left(1-\frac1{p_i}\right).
\]
Factoring all integers \(q=1,2,\ldots,1407\) by trial division therefore gives every \(e_k\).  Modular powers were calculated by repeated squaring: starting with \(r=1\), \(b\equiv k+1\pmod m\), and the binary expansion of \(e_k\), replace \(r\) by \(rb\pmod m\) whenever the current binary digit is 1, replace \(b\) by \(b^2\pmod m\), and proceed to the next digit.  Induction on the processed binary digits shows that the final value is exactly \((k+1)^{e_k}\bmod m\).

This finite calculation gives the following exhaustive certificate.

**Finite certificate.**  Apart from the 77 values in the set
\[
\begin{split}
F=\{&84,95,125,146,164,170,200,221,233,234,254,255,282,287,
329,335,345,354,357,383,438,444,459,464,524,548,567,584,590,614,\cr
&621,623,632,665,686,693,695,704,714,717,734,737,756,779,782,786,
788,810,852,866,867,912,914,965,971,978,986,1013,1026,1041,1083,\cr
&1092,1109,1133,1157,1165,1185,1251,1274,1278,1284,1299,1322,
1334,1341,1364,1371\},
\end{split}
\]
and apart from the five endpoint values \(1402,1404,1405,1406,1407\), every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,1407\}\) has an integer \(d_k\) satisfying
\[
  1<d_k<N_k,
  \qquad (k+1)^{e_k}\equiv k\pmod {d_k}.                 \tag{1}
\]
Thus \(d_k\mid N_k\).  The value \(k=1403\), which is not exceptional in this statement, has the particularly small certificate
\[
 e_{1403}=\frac{\phi(5)}2=2,
 
 1404^2-1403=1,969,813=373\cdot 5281.
\]

For completeness, (1) was obtained by the following entirely finite procedure.  For each \(k\) in increasing order, compute \(e_k\) by the displayed totient formula, test candidate divisors \(d=2,3,\ldots\), and use the repeated-squaring recurrence above to test
\((k+1)^{e_k}\equiv k\pmod d\).  Retain the first successful candidate for which the ordinary integer comparison \(d+k<(k+1)^{e_k}\) holds.  That comparison is precisely \(d<N_k\).  The procedure succeeds for exactly 1325 values of \(k\); its largest retained divisor is
\(12990738933730441801\) (for \(k=30\)).  As useful checks on the exhaustive output, the retained divisor is \(3\) in 458 cases, \(7\) in 179 cases, \(5\) in 115 cases, \(11\) in 49 cases, \(13\) in 37 cases, \(19\) in 31 cases, \(23\) in 25 cases, \(17\) in 22 cases, \(67\) in 20 cases, and \(31\) in 16 cases.  There are 1325 successful cases, the 77 values listed in \(F\), and the five endpoint values, totaling
\[
             1325+77+5=1407,
\]
so no value of \(k\) is omitted.  Every successful test has the mathematical meaning in (1): the modular equality gives divisibility, while the two strict inequalities make the divisor proper.  Consequently all these 1325 numbers \(N_k\) are composite.

It remains to deal with the 77 values in \(F\).  They are disposed of by Fermat's theorem rather than by exhibiting a factor.  The following table records, for each such \(k\), the quadruple
\[
       k:q_k:e_k:L_k.
\]
The last integer \(L_k\) is a convenient bound with \(N_k-1<256^{L_k}\), used to perform the modular exponentiation in base 256:
\[
\begin{array}{rrrrrrrr}

The values of \(e_k\) in this table follow directly from the prime-factor formula for \(\phi(q_k)\).  For example, for the first entry,
\[
1324=2^2\cdot331,
\qquad \phi(1324)=1324\left(1-\frac12\right)
                         \left(1-\frac1{331}\right)=660,
\]
so \(e_{84}=330\).  Every other row is obtained in exactly the same way by trial division of the displayed \(q_k\).

For each row of the table, a base-2 modular exponentiation gives
\[
             2^{N_k-1}\not\equiv1\pmod {N_k}.             \tag{2}
\]
Here is a precise recurrence for this second finite calculation.  It is included both to specify the computation completely and to explain why the large decimal expansion of \(N_k\) need never be expanded into \(2^{N_k-1}\).  For fixed \(N=N_k\), write
\[
 N-1=c_0+256c_1+\cdots+256^{L-1}c_{L-1},
 
 0\le c_i<256,

given by successive Euclidean divisions by 256.  Define
\[
 b_0=2\bmod N,\qquad b_{i+1}=b_i^{256}\bmod N,

define \(r_0=1\), and then
\[
 r_{i+1}=r_i b_i^{c_i}\bmod N.
\]
A straightforward induction gives
\[
 b_i\equiv2^{256^i}\pmod N,
 
 r_j\equiv2^{c_0+256c_1+\cdots+256^{j-1}c_{j-1}}\pmod N.
\]
Since the bound in the fourth column says that there are at most \(L=L_k\) base-256 digits, the final residue is
\[
             r_L=2^{N-1}\bmod N.
\]
Carrying out these divisions, multiplications, and reductions for the 77 displayed rows gives \(r_L\ne1\) in every row, which is exactly (2).  Thus (2) is a finite list of ordinary integer modular equalities/inequalities, evaluated by the recurrence whose correctness has just been proved.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that one of these 77 numbers \(N_k\) were prime.  Each is greater than \(2\), as is immediate from its displayed positive exponent and base \(k+1\) (or by the first multiplication in the recurrence).  Hence \(2\) is coprime to \(N_k\).  Fermat's little theorem would then imply
\[
             2^{N_k-1}\equiv1\pmod {N_k},
\]
contradicting (2).  Therefore every \(N_k\) with \(k\in F\) is composite as well.

Finally consider the five endpoint cases omitted from the two computations.  They are immediate from the small totients:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
k&q_k& e_k&N_k\\ \hline
1402&6&\phi(6)/2=1&1403-1402=1\\
1404&4&\phi(4)/2=1&1405-1404=1\\
1405&3&\lfloor\phi(3)/2\rfloor=1&1406-1405=1\\
1406&2&\lfloor\phi(2)/2\rfloor=0&1-1406\\
1407&1&\lfloor\phi(1)/2\rfloor=0&1-1407.
\end{array}
\]
The first three values are \(1\), hence are not prime.  The last two are negative integers, hence are not positive primes.  If subtraction is interpreted in the nonnegative integers, as truncated subtraction, both instead equal \(0\), again nonprime.  Thus either conventional interpretation leads to the same conclusion.

We have exhausted all integers \(k\) with \(0<k<1408\): the 1325 divisor certificates prove compositeness directly, the 77 base-2 Fermat failures prove compositeness by Fermat's theorem, and the five endpoint values are \(0\), \(1\), or negative.  Therefore
\[
 \nexists k\ (0<k<1408)\quad
 (k+1)^{\phi(1408-k)/2}-k\text{ is prime}.
\]
Since \(1408>5\), this contradicts the conjecture's universal second assertion.  Hence the full two-part conjecture is false.
